theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before the shift starts, what should the reception agent check?
options: The arrivals list, room status, keys and forms
The staff's personal phones and social media
The kitchen menu for the staff lunch break
The weather forecast for the next month

questions.stem: What should the reception desk look like before guests arrive?
options: Covered in staff bags, cups and personal papers
Full of guest files left open for anyone to see

With a smile, eye contact and a warm welcome

options: Tell them it is too late for a repair today

questions.stem: Who is "Team Jamaica" training for?
options: People who work with visitors to Jamaica

Farmers who grow crops for export

questions.stem: Why do first impressions at reception matter so much?
options: They decide how much the room will cost
They are the only thing guests remember

options: Ignore it, as it is not your job

options: Open it to see what it is

questions.stem: A letter arrives for a guest who checked out yesterday. What should you do?
options: Follow the policy: forward it or keep it safe
Throw it away, as the guest has gone
Give it to the next guest who stays in that room
Open it to find the guest's address

options: "Yeah?", and then wait for the caller to speak

options: Tell the guest it is their problem

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare the reception area at the start of a shift.
essays.modelAnswer: I arrive on time in a clean, full uniform with my name badge. I read the log book and the handover notes from the last shift, and ask about anything I do not understand. I print or open the arrivals list, the departures list and the room status report, and check with housekeeping which rooms are clean and ready. I check special requests for today's arrivals, such as a cot or an airport pick-up. I count and sign for my cash float, in J$ and US$ if both are used. I make sure there are enough registration cards, key folders, key cards, message pads, receipt books, pens and brochures. I check that the phone, computer, card machine and key encoder work. Finally, I tidy the desk so that no guest papers are on show, and I stand ready to greet the first guest with a smile.
markingPoints: On time, neat uniform and badge
Reads the log book and handover notes
Checks arrivals, departures, room status and special requests
Counts and signs for the float; stocks forms, keys and stationery
Checks equipment works; desk tidy with no guest papers on show

essays.stem: Describe the full check-in procedure for a guest who has a reservation.
essays.modelAnswer: I greet the guest with a smile, welcome them to the villa and ask for their name. I find the booking and confirm the dates, room type, rate, number of guests and any special requests. I ask for photo ID, such as a passport for an overseas guest, and check that the photo and name match the booking. The guest fills in and signs the registration card, and I check that it is complete and readable. I ask how they will pay and take a deposit or card pre-authorisation as the policy says, giving a receipt for any cash. I choose a clean, inspected room that matches the booking, encode the key cards and write the room number on the key folder, without saying it aloud. I explain breakfast times, Wi-Fi, the safe, the pool rules and how to call the desk. I then call the bell attendant or direct the guest to the room, wish them a pleasant stay and update the system.
markingPoints: Warm greeting; finds and confirms the booking details
Checks photo ID against the booking
Registration card completed and signed
Payment method set up (deposit or pre-authorisation) with a receipt
Clean room allocated, keys issued without saying the room number aloud; facilities explained; system updated

essays.stem: Explain why reception staff check guests' ID, and how to do it correctly and politely.
essays.modelAnswer: Reception checks ID to make sure that the person checking in is the person on the booking, to protect guests and their rooms, to prevent fraud with stolen cards, and because the property must keep correct records of who is staying, including the nationality of visitors. ID is also checked before giving a new key or any account information. To do it correctly, I ask politely, for example, "May I see your passport or a photo ID, please?" Overseas guests usually show a passport; Jamaican guests may show a passport, driver's licence or voter ID card, as the policy allows. I check that the photo looks like the guest, that the name matches the booking and the card used, and that the ID is in date. I copy only the details the policy asks for, never leave the ID lying on the desk, and hand it back at once with a thank you.
markingPoints: Reasons: right person, guest and room security, fraud prevention, correct records
ID also checked before new keys or account information
Asks politely
Checks photo, name and expiry date against the booking and card
Records only what the policy needs; returns the ID promptly and keeps it secure

essays.stem: Describe how to deal with a walk-in guest, from the greeting to giving them their key.
essays.modelAnswer: I greet the walk-in guest warmly and ask how many people are staying, for how many nights, and what kind of room they would like. I check the room status and the bookings to see which rooms are free and clean for all the nights asked. I offer suitable rooms and quote the rate clearly, with the meal plan, the currency and whether GCT is included at the current rate. If the guest agrees, I ask for photo ID and check it, and the guest fills in and signs a registration card. Because there is no booking or guarantee, I ask for payment in advance or a card pre-authorisation, as the policy says, and give a receipt. I open the guest's account in the system, encode the key cards and give them in a key folder with the room number written, not spoken. I explain the facilities, and arrange help with the luggage.
markingPoints: Greets and finds the needs (people, nights, room type)
Checks availability and room status
Quotes the rate clearly with meals, currency and tax
Checks ID; registration card signed; payment in advance or pre-authorisation with a receipt
Opens the account; issues keys privately; explains facilities

essays.stem: Explain how reception protects guests' privacy and security.
essays.modelAnswer: Reception never says a guest's room number aloud or gives it to anyone. The number is written on the key folder and shown only to the guest. If someone asks for a guest, by phone or in person, staff do not say whether the guest is staying or which room they are in; they offer to put the call through or take a message, and they call the guest before sending a visitor up. New keys are only made after checking ID against the registration, and lost key cards are cancelled. Registration cards, lists and folios are kept out of sight, the computer screen is locked when the desk is left, and card details are handled only in the secure system. Valuables are kept in the room safe or a front desk safe deposit box. Staff watch for people who do not belong, such as someone trying door handles, and report them to security or the supervisor at once.
markingPoints: Room numbers never said aloud or given out
Calls and visitors: no confirmation of guests; put through or take a message; call the guest first
ID checked before new keys; lost cards cancelled
Papers out of sight, screen locked, card details secure; safes for valuables
Watch for suspicious people and report them

essays.stem: Describe how to take a phone message for a guest who is out, and how to make sure the guest receives it.
essays.modelAnswer: I answer politely and, without saying whether the guest is in the property or their room number, I offer to take a message. I write on a message slip the guest's name, the caller's name and phone number, the message itself, the date and time, and my own name. I read the message back to the caller to check it, especially the phone number, and thank them. I then record the message in the system or the message book, and switch on the message light on the guest's room phone if the property has one. The slip is placed in a sealed envelope with the guest's name and kept at the desk, or delivered to the room as the policy says. When the guest returns, I give them the message privately. If the message is urgent, I try to reach the guest by the means the policy allows. Finally, I switch off the message light once it is delivered.
markingPoints: Does not confirm the room or presence; offers to take a message
Records guest, caller, number, message, date, time and own name
Reads the message back to the caller
Records it and switches on the message light; seals it in an envelope
Delivers it privately and promptly; switches off the light afterwards

essays.stem: Describe how you would deal with a guest who arrives early, before their room is ready.
essays.modelAnswer: I would welcome the guest warmly and thank them for arriving. I would check the room status and call housekeeping to ask when a suitable room will be ready, and whether another room of the same type is clean now. If a room is ready, I may check them in early, as the policy allows. If not, I would apologise and tell them honestly how long it should take. I would complete the registration, ID check and payment now, so that they only need to collect the key later. I would offer to store their luggage safely with a tag and a receipt, and suggest they relax by the pool, have a drink or lunch, or take a walk, and give them a towel if they want to swim. I would take their phone number or tell them where I will find them, and let them know as soon as the room is ready. I would note it in the log.
markingPoints: Warm welcome; checks status with housekeeping
Early check-in if a room is ready and policy allows; otherwise apologises and gives an honest time
Completes registration, ID and payment in advance
Stores luggage safely with a tag; offers facilities while they wait
Contacts the guest when the room is ready; notes it in the log

essays.stem: Describe the check-out procedure for a guest, including payment in J$ or US$.
essays.modelAnswer: I greet the guest by name and ask whether they enjoyed their stay. I check for any last charges, such as the minibar or breakfast, and make sure they are posted. I print the bill and give the guest time to check it, explaining any charges they ask about. If there is a mistake, I tell my supervisor so that it can be corrected. I ask how they will pay. If they pay in the other currency, for example US$ for a J$ bill, I use only the property's exchange rate for that day and show them the sum. I count cash in front of the guest, process cards as the procedure says, and give a receipt. I collect the room keys, check for any items in the safe deposit box, update the room status so housekeeping can clean the room, and offer help with luggage or a taxi. I thank the guest and invite them back.
markingPoints: Greets by name; checks and posts last charges
Prints the bill for the guest to check; queries handled or referred
Uses only the property's exchange rate for a different currency
Takes payment correctly, gives a receipt and collects keys
Updates room status, returns safe deposit items, offers help and thanks the guest

essays.stem: Explain how reception works with housekeeping and other departments, and why good communication matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Reception is the centre of information for guests. It tells housekeeping about arrivals, departures and room changes, so that rooms are cleaned in the right order, and it asks housekeeping for the room status so that only clean, inspected rooms are given to guests. It passes special requests, such as an extra bed, a cot or a late check-out, to the right department. It tells maintenance about faults that guests report, and the kitchen or the villa cook about allergies and special meals. It tells security about any worries, and the accounts office about charges. Good communication matters because guests get what they were promised, problems are fixed quickly, and staff do not waste time. Poor communication leads to guests being given dirty rooms, requests being forgotten and complaints. Reception should pass on messages clearly, record them in the log and check that they have been done.
markingPoints: Housekeeping: arrivals, departures, room changes and room status
Special requests passed to the right department
Maintenance, kitchen, security and accounts kept informed
Why: guests get what was promised; problems fixed quickly; fewer complaints
Messages passed on clearly, recorded and followed up

essays.stem: Describe what reception staff should do if the fire alarm sounds.
essays.modelAnswer: Reception staff must know the property's emergency procedure before an emergency happens, and follow it and the Centre's or property's rules exactly. When the fire alarm sounds, they stay calm and, if it is their duty, check the alarm panel to see where it is and call the fire service on the emergency number, giving the property's name, address and what is happening. They print or take the in-house list, the staff list and the visitors' book, and the master keys if that is their role. They help guide guests calmly to the exits and the assembly point, telling them not to use the lift or go back for belongings, and they give special help to guests with disabilities or small children. At the assembly point, they check the list to account for everyone, and tell the fire officers about anyone missing. Nobody goes back inside until the fire service says it is safe.
markingPoints: Knows and follows the emergency procedure; stays calm
Calls the fire service with clear details (if it is their duty)
Takes the in-house list, staff list, visitors' book (and master keys if their role)
Guides guests to the assembly point; no lifts; helps guests with special needs
Roll call at the assembly point; reports anyone missing; no re-entry until it is safe

practical1.title: Prepare the reception desk and check in guests (role play)
practical1.brief: Set up a reception desk in the Centre's training room for a made-up villa property. The assessor gives an arrivals list, a room status report, made-up bookings, a made-up exchange rate, made-up ID cards and a practice cash float in J$ and US$. As a group, prepare the desk: count and sign for the float, check the arrivals against the room status, prepare key folders and registration cards, and set out brochures and a facilities card. Then each member in turn checks in one "guest" (another member or the assessor), for example: an overseas couple with a booking who show passports; a Jamaican guest who shows a driver's licence and pays a J$ cash deposit; a walk-in guest who pays in US$ at the given rate; and a guest who arrives before their room is ready. Each check-in includes the greeting, finding and confirming the booking, the ID check, the registration card, the payment and receipt, choosing a ready room, issuing keys without saying the room number aloud, and explaining the facilities. Members who are not checking in play guests or the bell attendant. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, registration cards and receipts to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A reception desk with a computer (the Centre's training system) or paper forms
A made-up arrivals list, room status report and bookings (from the assessor)
Made-up ID cards and a practice cash float in J$ and US$, with a made-up exchange rate (from the assessor)
Registration cards, key folders, practice key cards, a receipt book and pens
Brochures and a facilities card for the villa
A phone or tablet to take the photos
photos: The float counted and signed for
The ID check, showing the made-up ID beside the booking
A completed, signed registration card for each guest
A receipt for each cash payment, including the US$ payment worked out at the given rate
The key folder with the room number written, not spoken
The early arrival: luggage tagged and stored
checklist: Helped prepare the desk and count the float correctly
Greeted the guest warmly with a smile and eye contact
Found the booking and confirmed the dates, room, rate and number of guests
Checked the ID properly and politely, and handed it back at once
Made sure the registration card was complete and signed
Took payment correctly, used the given exchange rate and gave a receipt
Allocated a clean, ready room and kept the room number private
Dealt with the early arrival or walk-in correctly and politely
safety: Use only made-up guest names, ID cards and practice money
Keep the float locked or in the drawer when it is not being used
Lift and store luggage with bent knees and a straight back
Keep cables and bags clear of the area in front of the desk

practical2.title: Reception shift tasks: calls, messages, keys, wake-up calls and a check-out (role play)
practical2.brief: Using the reception desk and the in-house guests from Practical 1 (or a made-up in-house list from the assessor), the group runs a reception shift. Each member in turn handles at least two tasks from the assessor's cards, with another member or the assessor as the guest, caller or visitor: a caller who asks for a guest's room number; a caller who leaves a message for a guest who is out; a visitor who wants to go to a guest's room; a guest who has lost their key card; a guest who wants a wake-up call; a guest who wants to put valuables in the safe deposit box; a guest who reports that the air conditioning is not working; and a guest who checks out and pays part in J$ and part in US$ at the made-up rate the assessor gives. Members record each task on the right form: message slip, wake-up call sheet, safe deposit record, maintenance report, log book and receipt. At the end, the group writes a handover sheet for the next shift. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and forms to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: The reception desk set-up from Practical 1, or a made-up in-house list (from the assessor)
Task cards and a made-up exchange rate (from the assessor)
Message slips and envelopes, a wake-up call sheet, a safe deposit record, a maintenance report form and a log book
A practice bill (folio) for the check-out, a receipt book and practice money in J$ and US$
A handover sheet, pens and a calculator
A phone or tablet to take the photos
photos: A call for a guest being handled without giving the room number
A completed message slip in a sealed, named envelope
The ID check before a new key card is made
The wake-up call sheet filled in
The safe deposit record signed by the guest
The maintenance report for the air conditioning
The check-out bill, the mixed-currency sum and the receipt
checklist: Kept room numbers and guest details private on every call and visit
Took a complete, correct message and made sure it would reach the guest privately
Checked ID before making a new key and cancelled the old one
Recorded the wake-up call correctly and read it back
Followed the safe deposit procedure, with the guest's signature
Reported the fault and told the guest what would happen
Checked the bill with the guest, worked out the mixed payment correctly and gave a receipt
Recorded each task correctly and helped write a clear handover sheet
safety: Use only made-up guest names, ID and practice money
Keep practice money and keys in the drawer or safe when not in use
Keep the desk and walkway clear of bags and cables
Shred or return all practice forms with guest details at the end
